name: Edward VI of England
summary: Edward VI was a boy king whose government was run by Somerset and then Northumberland, so the acts and Prayer Books issued in his name are not counted as his positions. His own papers show a committed Protestant who wanted idolatry abolished, church property and clergy brought under the crown and Mary's mass stopped, and who held a corporate view of the commonwealth in which excess wealth, enclosure, forestalling and luxury were abuses. His last personal act was the Devise for the Succession, which set aside the Act of Succession in favour of Lady Jane Grey.

sources.title: Literary Remains of King Edward the Sixth, vol. 2 (J.G. Nichols, ed.): Journal, Discourse on the Reformation of Abuses, draft acts, memorials, Devise for the Succession, minutes for his will

sources.usedFor: Identity (born 1537, died 1553), his minority, the Devise and his personal role in religion

property-fundamental.rationale: In his Discourse and draft acts he would cap holdings (two farms, 2,000 sheep, ceilings on wealth by occupation) and he wants forfeitures from those who have 'devoured their neighbours', which treats property rights as limited by the commonwealth.

more-religion-public.rationale: His Discourse wants everyone made to come to the prescribed service and those who swear, riot or neglect God's word duly punished; he lists godly education and the example of rulers as remedies.

revolution-justified.rationale: Inferred: his Discourse blames the 'disobedient and contentious talking and doing' of the common people and lists seditious bills among sores to be remedied, and his Journal calls the 1549 risers 'rebels'. He did not discuss revolution in general.

widespread-small-property.rationale: His Discourse says no one should hold more than two farms, two thousand sheep or more than the country can bear, and he blames engrossing and enclosure; an act against severing land from houses is in his draft list.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Inferred: his Discourse says a well-ordered commonwealth has every part obey one head, one governor and one law, and his Devise provides for hereditary heirs to the crown. He did not discuss monarchy as such.

separate-church-state.rationale: His own Discourse treats the church as one of the two parts of the realm's government, with discipline run by bishops under royal commission; his Journal has him requiring Mary to obey the religious service set by statute 'as a subject'.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: A Latin oration in his hand argues that adultery should be a capital offence on the strength of the Mosaic law and divine command, and his draft will wants godly ecclesiastical laws made and the canon laws abolished. The oration is a school exercise and the will text is in Petre's hand, so this is low.

single-common-good.rationale: His Discourse compares the commonwealth to a body whose parts must serve it, agree among themselves and not 'eat another up', with order, moderation and reason bridling affections. He does not discuss balancing group interests.

rule-by-example.rationale: Discourse lists 'example of rulers' as one of eight remedies and wants justices who share the vices punished by new laws removed, but also relies on new laws, strict execution and punishment, so the evidence points both ways.

class-collaboration.rationale: His Discourse lists 'engendering friendship in all the parts of the commonwealth' as a remedy and describes gentlemen, merchants, artisans and husbandmen as limbs that must each use their gain so the others can do their service.

ban-interest.rationale: His Discourse names exchange and usury among the sores of the commonwealth to be cured by good laws strictly executed; it does not say interest must be banned outright, and the 1552 statute against interest was Parliament's.

trade-surplus.rationale: No recorded position found. (Reviewer: favouring bullion-bringing trade at a mart is nearby evidence, not a stated aim of exporting more than importing.)

church-by-bishops.rationale: His Discourse wants church discipline carried out in each diocese by the best of the bishops under royal commission and wants worthy men appointed bishops; he never compared this with congregational government, so it is low.

death-penalty.rationale: In his own hand (Jan 1552) he wanted Somerset and his confederates punished and executed according to law as an example; he drafted an act making export of bullion a felony; a Latin oration argues the magistrate bears the sword and may punish grave crimes with death.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Journal: after long tolerance 'against my will' he told Mary he constrained not her faith but willed her, as a subject, to obey, and refused the Emperor's ambassador's request that she keep her mass; he would not let her services be exempt from the statute.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Discourse: it is convenient to enrich the country but hurtful to enrich any one part immoderately, and no person may have more than the commonwealth can bear.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: In his own hand he listed gathering and coining church plate, selling chantry and college lands, and having patrons and clergy bound by statute (no reserving of benefice income, no church leases beyond 21 years). He also wanted discipline exercised only by bishops he picked and commissioned.

character-from-environment.rationale: Discourse: quoting Horace's image of the new vessel keeping the savour of what it was first filled with, he says 'for the most part men be as they be brought up', and makes good education the first remedy. A pair of school orations argues both sides of whether people are evil by nature.

ban-cartels.rationale: He proposed acts against regrating and forestalling and against holding more than a set number of farms, and the Discourse denounces those who forestall markets to raise prices. His motive is fair prices and distribution rather than competition as such.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: His draft apparel act reserves cloth of gold and purple to the blood royal and grades other materials by rank, and his Discourse warns that the decline of the landed nobility's income will ruin that estate.

elective-rulers.rationale: Inferred: his Devise settles the crown on named hereditary heirs (heirs male of his cousins) and nowhere contemplates election of rulers.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: His Discourse lists excess in apparel, diet and building among the sores of the commonwealth, and he wrote a bill restraining dress by rank.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: His Journal records that he pressed his sister Mary to stop hearing mass, said he could no longer tolerate it, and notes the bishops' conclusion that licensing sin was sin; it also records people sent to prison for hearing mass. Mass was held privately in her household, and he gave no general doctrine, hence low.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Inferred: his Devise begins 'for lack of issue of my body', treating issue of his body as the first in line, and then names heirs in turn; there is no statement on the principle itself.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: His Discourse wants the many statutes brought into one short, plain body so people can understand them and wants the laws executed justly without respect of persons; it does not address decrees.

capital-controls.rationale: He drafted an act making carrying bullion out of the realm a felony, listed conveying bullion and goods abroad among the commonwealth's sores, and proposed prohibiting export of horses.

notes: Minority rule: acts of Parliament, the Prayer Books, proclamations and council measures in his name were not counted. School orations are exercises on set themes (some argue both sides), so they are used only as low-confidence support. His Journal is mostly a terse record of events, so entries are used only where it records his own stance (Mary's mass, Somerset's execution, the council's price rebuke). Left null: price controls (the Journal only records council proclamations), the Devise's legality and Parliament's role (known mainly from Chief Justice Montagu's later account), and the 1549 Somerset-era enclosure policy (his own sympathies are inferred only by a footnote).
